headline: Popular AI tools often wrongly judged whether home blood pressure monitors had passed clinical accuracy testing, a preliminary study found.
score_reason: Useful consumer-health finding, but a preliminary abstract presented on 8 Oct 2026, so lowered by 1 as slightly stale.
importance_line: People who buy home blood pressure monitors after asking a chatbot are affected first, then doctors who advise them, but the work is an unreviewed abstract and the tools may have improved since the April-May 2026 tests.
summary: The American Heart Association reports, from a study presented at its Hypertension Scientific Sessions, that ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Perplexity correctly said whether a home blood pressure monitor had been clinically validated only about 63% to 83% of the time, while Google Gemini scored 86% to 91%, across 324 monitors tested in Canada. The findings are an abstract that has not been peer-reviewed, and the researchers advise checking monitors against independent public registries.
notes: Read the AHA release, the original source; HealthDay (pool link) carried the same study on 9 Oct 2026 but its page gave no text. 'Validated' means independent testing showed accurate readings.
